comments.name: Ima Palled
comments.body:
When I was a kid, my grandfather used to send me audio letters on cassette tapes. He never broke the habit of speaking into the tape recorder as he would when talking into his Dictaphone for a secretary to later transcribe into a typed, paper letter. His audio letters thus sounded like this: 

"Hope you are having fun at camp (period). Yesterday (comma), your grandmother and I visited Sheila (comma), whose first question was (open quotation marks), "How are the grandchildren (question mark, close quotation marks)?" 

"(Paragraph) Looking forward to seeing you soon (exclamation point, period.)" 

Anyone who ever heard and remembers the kind of dictation that was necessary sixty years ago can appreciate the role that artificial intelligence has in allowing Whispr Flow and similar applications to more easily and intuitively convert text to speech. Note, though, that my grandfather was dictating simple business letters to his secretary via a machine that allowed him to work when she was not present; he was knowingly not composing great literature. There is a valid place for technologal aid such as this, so long as one understands the proper use and limits of the technology. Those who are sufficiently naive as to believe that stream-of-consciousness dictation equals great writing do so at our collective cultural peril.

For the benefit of the readers, these talks aren't solely about trade; they are about whether Canada will be a self-governing country with agency over its economy, or a vassal state to the US. There is much of the latter already and that explains the objectionably imperious attitude of the US negotiators. 

The American Ambassador to Canada, unpopular as he may be, has had the virtue of periodic clarity about what the REAL issues are: (1) priority access to Canadian rare minerals, (2) exclusivity at a discount on Canadian oil, (3) the F-35 fighter jet contract, (4) the restoration of American booze on the shelves of the liquor commissions, and (5) the dismantling of dairy supply management in Canada as needed for unfettered US access to the Canadian dairy market. There may be others, but those are the key ones, and they strike at the heart of Canada's economic sovereignty. 

As well Canada is loathe to make piece-meal concessions that pit one province against the other, given how regionally-based various Canadian industries happen to be. That is why Canada needs a comprehensive agreement - to keep the country together, contrary to the US interest to dismember it. 

Also important is a serious question about whether anything signed with this Administration will be respected, and how an agreement can provide perfected security about that. 

This is the real meat of what's going on. It's much less about 50% tariffs on hockey sticks.

No one gets the nomination (usually bestowed in a closed party convention) unless the plaintiffs' bar gives the okay.  The same requirement applies for appointments to the bench when there is a vacancy.  Judges are therefore beholden to plaintiffs' attorneys, as are most other elected official in this state.  Judges routinely ignore rules of procedure and statutory safeguards in order to favor plaintiffs; trial rulings consistently favor one side and punish the other; relevant evidence is kept from juries; fabricated opinion evidence is allowed, and appeals to higher courts linger for up to three years, thus enabling the worst kind of lawyers to prosper at the expense of justice. This is a step towards "personalized medicine" which had been tantalizing us since the era of DNA sequencing started. 
Cancers, even under the same classification, like melanomas, typically exhibit one of a few mutations, and proper treatment depends on which one. This technology allows precise targeting of the individual mutation involved, with minimal side effects to other cells. An individual vaccine against the individual cancer case can be created by the mRNA technique, which allows very rapid development of the desired specificity, without having to change the basic structure of the vaccine, which would require slow development and testing. 
This means, however, that it's not a general vaccine to prevent cancer; since it requires knowing the DNA sequence of the cancer in question, it's for attacking a cancer which has appeared, in this study in conjunction with surgical removal.

comments.name: Judy
comments.body: Neurofeedback (NFT) is a non-invasive non-drug treatment that re-programs areas of the brain to work at a healthy pace.  Some areas go far too fast and produce anxiety, distractability, and sometimes angry acting out.  Other areas go too slowly and that results in depression.  A brain map, made by recording brain waves from the brain identifies areas that are either too sluggish or too speedy.  Treatment is by putting sensors over targeted areas and programming a computer to give a sensory "reward" when the bundle(s) of neurons in that area fire at the optimum speed, not too slowly, not too fast.  The reward can be a sound, a blink on a screen, or any perceptible stimulus.  It happens very fast and not by conscious control--the patient sits quietly, often watching tv, for 30-minute treatments with a trained professional.  Gradually the targeted neurons fire at the desired speed and the patient's experience does too--less lethargy, depression, or explosions, more positive mood.  It seems magical for children whose behavior is out of control--they watch a favorite tv show during treatments and gradually they stop acting out.  Adults "feel better" and can lead normal lives. All of this with NOTHING put into the body--no drugs, no shocks, no electricity introduced into the brain.  Just sensing what specific areas are doing and rewarding them for "doing better."   NFT saved my life after 70+ years of CPTSD craziness and suffering.   Google it!

comments.name: A. Raymond
comments.body: Several years ago I ordered a Lyft from SFO airport to my home. The Lyft app informed me that the driver had arrived but I didn’t see the car  close by. Then it showed me taking the Lyft and dropping me off a mile from the airport ( far from my home). I had to take a Uber  home. Lyft charged me. I  complained to Lyft that the ride never occurred on the online app. They dismissed it. And there was no way to reach an actual customer service person. My credit  card company reversed the charges ( which is also not straightforward). Now, I never take Lyft.

comments.name: Neil Bellinson
comments.body:
Seems to me that Lyft should be forced to pay many hundreds, if not a few thousand dollars in penalties for each violation for what is clearly a scam.

In New York City, perhaps Mayor Mamdani could do something to enact a regulation to achieve this.

As far as taking photos is concerned, one might try this instead: just before exiting your ride, use your cell phone to take a VIDEO showing the back seat, the driver (or at least the driver's back), continuing to film after getting out, showing the license plate and, finally, showing the car driving away.

Filming the car driving away is important so that Lyft cannot claim you took the video at the start of the ride.

Seems to me that such a video would be very helpful in a criminal trial against Lyft and/or the driver which might result in heavy financial penalties and even jail time.

comments.name: Nick
comments.body:
Somewhat related:

Last week I stayed in a hotel whose rooms weren't that great. Warning signs about being charged for what they considered misdemeanors. The front desk person was chilly and the place looked a bit down at heel. I got the sense that these people would take anyone to the cleaners if they could. So I did something I've never done before: take a half dozen photos of the room as I left. People do this with rented cars, so why not?

I realize that this places a burden on the consumer and that that isn't really fair. But it helps to avoid exactly these exasperating situations the article describes.

comments.name: CK
comments.body: I left Lyft years ago after a billing dispute - I was charged much more (like three times more) than the price I had accepted in the app and I got zero help from customer service. Uber has been really bad lately, as others have noted: always incorrect wait times, expensive, and constant cancelations. So I went back to traditional cabs at least from the airport, though was then reminded why ride-shares took off in the first place: cabs have their own issues. So no good options really. I do use other ride-share services in other countries, most recently Grab in Singapore. It's usually pretty quick and painless to set up the app and depending where you are, using a ride-share service alleviates any potential language struggles or payment confusion as opposed to a traditional cab.

comments.name: Chad

Oh, the maddening world of "customer service" so prevalent lately. 

Funny that the driver had already been deactivated for other reasons by the time this was resolved. Perhaps a better response could have prevented others being similarly abused?

comments.name: AAT
comments.body:
While this case appears to involve mistaken identity or driver fraud, I’d like to share a few thoughts as a part-time Uber driver.

It's important to understand that Uber and Lyft drivers use their own personal vehicles—our everyday cars—to provide service. Having to deal with situations like vomiting inside or outside the vehicle is extremely unpleasant. When that happens, we have to stop accepting rides, find a place to clean the car, or take time off to get it professionally cleaned. Who covers these cleaning costs and the income lost during that time? A $150 payout is hardly sufficient. For example, I experienced this on a Friday night and ended up losing the entire Saturday cleaning and shampooing my car to remove stains and odors. Uber reimbursed me only $80, and I have no idea what they charged the rider.

Additionally, while smartphones often have geolocation features that can tag photos with location data, some of us disable this for privacy reasons. I do. So, if you're trying to find location info in my pictures, you won’t find any. 

And yes, Uber’s customer service responses—whether to drivers or riders—are often boilerplate or AI-generated, which can be frustrating.

comments.body: I hope the Russians don’t have a hand in this. and that it’s just the messy territory that comes with a functioning democracy.

While the reporting itself is informative (and in line with what we have learned in the past about some of the key figures) questions remain. If the war is going as well from Ukraine's perspective as we're being led to believe, why the military shake up at this particular juncture - even taking into consideration possible personal rivalries? How deep is the corruption alluded to and whom does it touch? Lastly, if there is to be a power upset at the very top in Ukraine (removal of Zelensky), is there any prospective replacement who will run on ending this war as soon as possible by finding a diplomatic path to peace, as polling indicates a majority of ordinary Ukrainians desperately want?

He contested the election of 1864 vigorously, but he was always prepared for the possibility that he might lose, which for time seemed to be likely.  Even so, he never blocked the elections.

Thank you Damien for covering this piece, in such comprehensive details.

There was no news report about this event on official media channels from Vietnam. It's a shame we have to turn to foreign respectable news outlets to get a full coverage of what happened. 

Justice wasn't served (yet), but the youth is now paying more attention to what is happening in our homeland. I think that's a great step forward. May the force be with us.

comments.name: NoName
comments.body:
Thank you for your report on the incident regarding the Community Party official. This story highlights a significant concern for many of us living in Vietnam.
​Beyond the specific details of this crash, many citizens here feel a profound sense of helplessness when facing those in positions of power who often act with impunity. There is a widespread, systemic issue where individuals are frequently oppressed or silenced when they seek justice against those with authority.
​I am reaching out to express my hope that international media outlets like The New York Times will continue to investigate these patterns of behavior. By bringing broader visibility to the lack of accountability and the challenges faced by ordinary citizens in Vietnam, you can provide much-needed support for the cause of transparency and human rights. We hope such coverage encourages international oversight and prompts necessary reforms to ensure that no one is above the law.

comments.name: Tadhg
comments.body:
What's worse - a 2-party state that where the ruling party only prosecutes its political opponents? Or a 1-party state that never prosecutes its own?

China wouldn't hesitate to make an example of this pathetic human because they understand the power of public perception, whereas Vietnam is just shooting itself in the foot and inviting further public discontent.

Many comparisons to be made...

comments.body: It is great to see Africans owning the value chain in lucrative industries, where they have mostly been suppliers of the raw materials that made the finished products they ended up buying from developed nations. I understand why some get repulsed by his riches, but to his credit, Dangote has been a catalyst and a partner in injecting capital into many viable initiatives in Africa. More than this article lists, Dangote is strategically helping alleviate African nations’ transportation and digital infrastructure needs, as well as dependence on food and energy imports.  His conglomerate is investing in multiple commercial data center hubs and power plants (Tanzania & Gambia), a sugar refinery in Nigeria, Africa’s largest fertilizer plant in Ethiopia, and fuel tank storage farms in Guinea and Djibouti. If the global crises send him the windfalls that make him richer, I commend him for his well-timed and strategic investments and wish him more success. Nigerians and the rest of Africans should rally around him and support any well-meaning homegrown investors by building the institutions and codifying laws that protect their investments for the long haul.

Then for almost  15 years, we went to the beaches in Provincetown, MA.  In both Rhode Island and Massachusetts, you have to lug all of your stuff from home to the beach.  We now live in Italy and go to the beaches in Forte dei Marmi and I have to say, we prefer the beach clubs to all of the beaches we used to frequent.  A day at the beach in Forte dei Marmi is more than wonderful.  We park our car in the free  covered lot where it does not fry while you are on the beach. The only thing that needs to be carried is a small beach bag and even that is not really necessary since everything is provided for you at the beach clubs.......a tent with loungers, chairs, and a table, a lock box to store your personal items when you go swimming, huge fluffy beach towels, table service right on the beach and if you choose to eat lunch, a restaurant offering excellent local dishes, a personal changing cabana with with more fluffy towels with your own key, impeccably kept bathrooms alongside the cabanas, shaded seating areas to lounge in with oversized comfortable chairs and hammocks, and on top of all of that, a big, pristine pool to swim in.  Yes, of course this is not free, you have to pay a fee for these services but it is more than worth it because you get so much for that fee.  We usually go to the same beach club every summer and it is never crowded.

comments.name: Brent Jatko
comments.body: Has anyone asked the mayor what's in it for him?

comments.name: Barry S
comments.body: No map is necessary. Everybody knows exactly where the Ligurian Sea is.

comments.name: RLA
comments.body: I’m an American living in Italy for a few years.  I used to think the beach club system in Italy was quirky but kind of charming.  But my experience has been that the clubs are crowded, expensive and patrons are proprietary about their position on the sand, day after day.  Also, the closer your umbrella is to the water, the more expensive the rent.  The so-called public beach in most towns is usually on the end next to the jetty, is even more crowded and feels like a second class experience.  The whole system needs to be jettisoned, but that of course will never happen.  There is money to be made.  The mountains call.

comments.name: Lou
comments.body: The whole beach club setup seems icky and not much fun. Go to France if you want nice beaches.

comments.name: Seasocal
comments.body:
It is not a beach with all those regimented lined up lounges and umbrellas, it is a parking lot.  

Let the beach be open space, schlep your own modest amount of stuff and respect the other users.

This perversion of public space is spreading here, except in its typical American Way, example: the selfish giant pavilions held down by sandbags for two people to sit under cordoning off 100 sq ft.  These are either set up by app based "beach services" (example Hanalei, HI) or part of the massive amount of stuff trundled down to the sand by the giant tire off road beach wagons from Costco in S. Cal.

comments.name: B
comments.body: How does anyone enjoy going to a beach packed with so many umbrellas you can't see the ocean, or even have a little peace and quiet away from the crowds? See the museums, avoid the beaches.

articles.title: In Italy, a Beach Club Run by Nuns Is in Jeopardy
articles.summary: The Sisters of Charity of Saint Mary have hosted beachgoers in the town of Spotorno for decades. But change is coming.

comments.name: Melanie H.
comments.body: Line dancing helps me stay active and meet friends. The group I dance with is filled with really kind people, ages 55 up to mid 80s. We hug and smile and are interested in each other. It's my fave day of the week!

comments.name: Angelina
comments.body: 'Enter the Sandman' - Metallica. My fantasy Walkup song!

comments.name: John Virgone
comments.body: Nothing like a local hiking/camping trip deep in the woods concomitant with a daily six pack, followed by a smoky cup of lapsang souchong while listening to Pink Floyd's "Brain Damage/Eclipse"; and, through and through, living deliberately.

comments.name: Didrah
comments.body: Walk Up song: Welcome to the Jungle. I worked for Guns n Roses for a year, and when that lone guitar starts in the dark arena, and 150,000 people start screaming, there is NOTHING like it. A good thing, was taking (newly 13) girl and a bestie to San Diego to see Noah Kahan at Petco Park - seeing her and 10s of thousands rock out to a classic singer/songwriter who plays acoustic guitar and has a fiddle player (female!) and features mandolin heavily was amazing! She held stood up the entire time (while also holding my hand). Good music, well written, beautifully performed, is alive and out there, and selling out stadiums, contrary to reports otherwise! Finding boatloads of Lindt 70% chocolate bars for sale at Grocery Outlet, for 4$...WHOO HOO! It's been a good week! Thanks for all of these other things to explore and celebrate. :)

comments.name: Joanz
comments.body: I love that you shared “the third thing”. It’s such a romantic yet grounded way of thinking about love.

comments.name: Kathy McAvoy
comments.body: Part of my job is to manage the social media for my employer. But our business page is linked to my personal LinkedIn page. So, on my personal page I post twice per week: "Miracle Mondays" which start the week off with positivity, and "What's-Your-Why?" Wednesdays, to remember the passion that drives us. And it's getting a great response!

comments.name: I Am
comments.body:
The reason for all the suffering/dissatisfaction in the world is due to the conditioning associated with the assumption of fundamental separation. From this perspective, fundamental separation isn't findable, particularly between "me" and "everything else". 

When the conditioning associated with the assumption of fundamental separation dissolves, then it is recognized that joy/happiness is the default. 

Pain, desire, thoughts, and ordinary human emotions may still appear, intimately and deeply felt. They are not obstacles. Acceptance and freedom, love and bliss, ecstasy and peace, doesn't appear to depend on their absence. It is not something that needs to be maintained, nor does there appear any efforting to maintain it.

comments.name: Amanda
comments.body: I’d not heard of Love Letters. Such kindness. A great org I write with is called Letters Against Isolation. Great mission of writing to seniors who are often lonely. I also have penpals through LEX (the letter exchange) so I get a bit of mail in my mailbox too.

articles.title: The Good List: 6 Things to Add Some Joy to Your Day
articles.summary: Walk-up songs, a shopping app and a despair antidote.

comments.name: Tom
comments.body: Was the Presidential autopen a precursor of what is to come?

comments.name: Jamakaya
comments.body: In this vein but concerned with more than liberal democracy is Aurora Linnea's "Man Against Being: Body Horror and the Death of Life." It takes on body hatred, the destruction of nature and Man's mad quest to transcend his mortal flesh, now dragging us all along into the final evolution of transhumanism. It's in the eco-feminist tradition of Susan Griffin's "Woman and Nature" but with real teeth. I'm not connected to the book in any way, just thought it was a terrific read and may interest others concerned about our current trajectory.

comments.name: Steve Sailer
comments.body: This sounds more like a Young Adult novel than a serious work of nonfiction.

comments.name: CEC
comments.body: Perhaps not an original thought but decisions made every day at increasing frequency and speed appear to be leading our society back to a feudalist state in which tech lords control all, subjecting the rest of us to literal serfdom. Our society's current massive income inequality appears to be the onramp to a looming neo-feudalism.

comments.name: Louise Yarnall
comments.body: Skepticism is healthy, and there indeed are some irresponsible tech company leaders showing glib indifference toward the principles of American democracy. So I understand concern. At the same time, half the voters in this country were well on the way to a stunning embrace of anti-democratic ideas and untruthful candidates largely through their personal choice to consume one-sided information from cable TV, chain emails, and online biased media sources that fail to follow any basic precepts of the Fourth Estate. Among my family and neighbors, those who cast votes in this manner haven’t been big users of AI. So while I understand the author’s concern around an AI authoritarian state, I think we have deeper problems that begin with each of us. I see the generally passive approach to media consumption as part of the problem—and perhaps also that so many of us are so overwhelmed by the challenges of just making a living and supporting families to track civic information effectively. If there’s any way to put AI in the service of citizens so they can pierce the propaganda bubbles and manage information overload, that would be a potential good thing. Going back to town meetings sounds fine—and we all should do that too. But in my experience over 40 years, those meetings can be quite problematic too. More often than we’d like to admit, such meetings offer an opportunity to witness up close how strident, disrespectful, and unkind we have become as a people.

comments.name: BJ
comments.body: Machines do stuff that humans invented to be done. Fair enough. But what if humans don’t know how stuff is done by a machine? Then humans can’t evaluate the quality or accuracy of the work, just the efficiency of the machine in arriving at an answer, however possibly flawed. Sort of like teaching a fine tennis swing without caring if the ball clears the net. Without parallel human processes, it’s all about technique.

comments.name: Gaucho
comments.body: I look forward to AI solving problems in the medical field and in a few other areas but in the grand scheme of things, it seems like the “internet age” has delivered a lot of over-valued companies that haven’t made our lives much better, just different and annoying in new and unusual ways. I’d take a 90’s style hang with low-potency THC and macro beers with my fellow humans over whatever the heck we have now any day of the week and twice on Sunday…

comments.name: David Weinberg
comments.body:
Lepore seems to miss the point. 
She often does, by the way. It isn’t AI that is the problem. Whether you have a group of 15 experts or a super fast processor making decisions doesn’t matter. Logically AI would do a better job. The problem is the centralization of vast decision making by the market place being entrusted to a government authority. It’s that rule by everybody becomes rule by the Government. It is the end of individual freedom.

articles.title: A Government for the People, but Not by People
articles.summary: In a new book, Jill Lepore examines what happens when we abandon liberal democracy for rule by automation and machines.

comments.name: Logic
comments.body:
Science is the only way forward, economically and culturally.
Everything else is largely a waste of time.

comments.name: Daniel Kazakos
comments.body: @Patricia I personally pitched my AI startup idea to Malta and the Y combinator. Both passed. What I found out from the process is that both these large scale initiatives or brand names lack the incubation necessary to cultivate the changes we want to see. It really takes an eco-system of innovators to reach a critical mass of failures vs successes for real growth. I'm still bullish on my AI startup in Malta, but the path forward for funding is not as clear. It really is just a matter of politics and preference that is driving me there. Which was another NY Times article about young talent moving away from the US.

comments.name: smith
comments.body: Europe wants a breakthrough.  It wants to achieve a breakthrough in a European way.  That means no one works on weekends and holidays.  Everyone enjoys a prolonged vacation.  No one can earn a lot more than the average, especially in terms of after tax take-home incomes.  Finally and most importantly, if you succeed at a breakthrough, most of the profits have nothing to do with you.  They go straight to the government which will leverage it up with borrowings and then give everything to those who do nothing.

comments.name: Robert Alen Richter
comments.body: I was wondering about that "trillion dollar investment gap". Does this include the massive sums being pumped into the AI bubble?

comments.name: LilaLeela
comments.body: Good luck Europe.  I sure hope you can lead.  I still admire that you mostly have the Greater Good for your people.  For example I love how you ‘fine’ tech companies. I wish the US would target tech and make them pay their fair share.

comments.name: Reedman
comments.body: If you want to build any physical item (in the EU or elsewhere), you need large quantities of affordable, reliable electric power. The EU doesn't have that. If you want people to show up for work, you have to have air conditioning, and not have 6 weeks vacation. If you want a "good job" in the EU, you want a government job, not a technology job. If you want to rent an apartment in Paris, the landlord will require you (or someone else) with a guaranteed job or pension to sign the lease.

articles.title: Europe Pushes for Moonshot Breakthroughs to Compete With China and U.S.
articles.summary: European governments, facing a nearly $1 trillion gap in investment funding, are casting a wide net to back start-ups developing pioneering technologies.

comments.name: Guido
comments.body:
Amen
Does it really matter?
Of course it does.
Especially when those spoken last
Become those spoken first
As the journeys that end
Are also the beginnings of crossing beyond
To whatever occurs next

Sam Roberts is a spiritual mensch
With a wit much drier than the driest Martini

Cheers to you, Sir!
Many Happy Returns ...

comments.name: kris
comments.body: I cannot wait to read this!

comments.name: TW
comments.body: To Mr. Sam Roberts, a clever writer in his own right:  if you could plan your own last words, what would they be?

comments.name: David Z.
comments.body: My favorite has to be Pancho Villa's last words: "Tell them I said something interesting." - not sure where I picked up this nugget or if it's accurate! :)

comments.name: A Texan in Vermont
comments.body:
Lovely article until the end, with a needless spoiler for Citizen Kane. I’m so glad I first saw that movie without knowing the meaning of “Rosebud” until the revelation at the end. It’s a great moment that shouldn’t be spoiled. Also, Kane’s nurse rushes into the room immediately after he says it, implying that she heard the word and is responding. I’ve always assumed that she’s the person who reported “Rosebud” to the reporters.

Remember, there are always folks out there who haven’t seen Citizen Kane yet.

comments.name: rfrawley
comments.body: I don't know if it was his literal last words, but I've read that when Bob Hope was on his deathbed, his wife asked him what he'd like to have on his tombstone. "Oh, I don't know," he replied, "surprise me."

comments.name: Photogirl
comments.body:
I've been lifelong friends with a hypochondriac, and I always joke with our mutual friends that we'll need to get "I told you I was sick!" engraved on his tombstone. (Yes, I know that a Floridian who died in 1979 already claimed it, but it's just so great.)

Now if we can only convince him to say those actual words on his deathbed! (Uh-oh...I hope I haven't jinxed him.)

comments.name: Chance
comments.body:
Charlie Munger's last words were spoken at the hospital. 
When the nurse asked "How are you, Mr. Munger?"
He responded "I'm dying. How are you?"

articles.summary: Determining the reliability of final thoughts can be a challenge when conveying a person’s life story on deadline.

comments.name: Mondoman
comments.body: Sadly no real details on the propulsion system of the rescue spacecraft here. From the mention of xenon gas, it sounds like it is an electric ion propulsion engine, in theory much more efficient than the chemical rockets and thrusters commonly used.

comments.name: Jeff
comments.body: Was Katalyst selected via a no-bid contract? Does the company ownership have financial connections to the Trump family? Unfortunately, these need to be standard questions reporters ask these days.

comments.name: Jim Toft
comments.body:
Much valid criticism of the squandering of $30m in this valiant attempt to extend the useful life of the Swift platform. But also consider what has been learned and will serve engineers and administrators in future, innovative endeavors. It’s inspirational.

Comparatively, utilizing the DoD estimate for Iran theater operations, $30million is being consumed every two+ hours. At least with an unsuccessful satellite effort, we have accrued more knowledge by aiming up and not at.

comments.name: Ray Wisman
comments.body: Hats off to the engineers at NASA, who exceeded requirements by 20 years, and Katalyst Space Technologies, that under extremely limited time, came close and undoubtedly learned much useful data for capturing other satellites. That $30 million spent gained much more than the many munitions fired off in Iran.

comments.name: Rick Graham
comments.body: Keep trying you engineers for the future of exploration ---interesting how to manage the 11-year cycle of the sunspots for future goals. My tax dollars well spent --rather than the military-industrial-complex.

"Last September, NASA hired a small company, Katalyst Space Technologies, of Flagstaff, Ariz., for $30 million to put together a mission to save Swift on an extremely rushed schedule."

Another no-bid contract with an unqualified vendor?

comments.name: Seattlite

comments.name: Scott Cee
comments.body:
No, no they don't have a right of grievance for debt, cost of living.  Deal with it, pay off your debt, live within your means, or gasp, work harder.

It's what every generation before who made this country great did, not grievance about it...

comments.name: David Graf
comments.body: If Ms. Josephson or Ms. Dinan want students to forsake communities, they need only require them to pay the full cost of their “education” instead of foisting it off on taxpayers via unpaid student loans.

comments.name: Melissa Kauth
comments.body: Was this the warmth of collectivism Susan speaks about?  No thanks.

comments.name: Tom O'Hare
comments.body: First letter nails it: many young people in college have no idea what it took to build the world they are so incredibly lucky to live in. They are spoiled, and many of their dimwit professors can only tell them how "unjust" things are in America as the fruits of capitalism fill in said professors' 401ks. As for the second letter, it simply makes no sense.

comments.name: Steven Yedlin
comments.body: They fail to note that  extreme concentrations of wealth have all the same bad effects as socialism.

comments.name: Allyn Klunder
comments.body: Probably a good indicator of our societal timeline. If you think of it like an individual,  we might be 60+. Relatively, what we do in the next 5 - 10 years will determine if we reach 90 or exit much sooner.

comments.name: Paul Manner
comments.body: I love the fact that we have a dean from Adelphi who responds to the observation “Universities operate as a closed economy: centrally administered, collectively resourced, carefully controlled by administrators who hope their plans aid retention efforts” by essentially confirming said observation!

comments.name: Matthew F
comments.body: Two perfect letters worth publishing: the first reminds us of the virtues of hard work, initiative and personal effort, while the second tries to sell us the tired bromide of “community.” Ms Russy shows us the danger of not passing along to the next generation the need to create wealth not just take it. As Thomas Sowell put it, the true miracle of capitalism is prosperity (poverty and toil being the natural state of man) and people who reverse them suffer the consequences. Ms Dinah’s letter is the best example of the confused belief in “communities over individuals” as if a community were anything more than a collection of individuals. She also forgets that communities don’t always produce success: they also produce homelessness, tax burdens, and ignorance (as community schools have generated for decades in America)

comments.name: Incognito in the city
comments.body: Wonderful to read about Opa Werner’s zest for life! Wishing him many happy and healthy years of fun ahead!

comments.name: Vero
comments.body: His accent is Berlin, which adds even more curmudgeon ! ( Berliners are famous for being “ grumpy but friendly”)

comments.name: Dksmvy
comments.body: He’s good for the soul!

comments.name: Mitchell Hammond
comments.body: I just have to say it... Germans have, in North America at least, a certain reputation as sticks-in-the-mud. But scratch a bit and it ain't always so. Plus we should never tire of old folks having fun and watching young folks enjoy them do it. Go Werner!

comments.name: Helen
comments.body: Omg 64 is not old!!!  It’s running half marathons and hiking Patagonia. Yes 89 is up there. Let’s call it early third act. Swimming and yoga. Older people are just people. Please understand they are just 45 year olds stuck in sometimes slower bodies.

comments.name: LNick
comments.body:
I would love to see NYT develop an over 60 (or even an over 80) column and highlight life for older folks. They are becoming a majority and their charms and life experience are valuable and enormous and good for younger people to read about. My dad at 92 has bloomed to have a bit of a younger fan club since my mom died, similar to this fellow. He is a favorite partner at pickleball (since he can still beat them) where all the players are younger, my sister (age 58) friends have basically adopted him, invite him to social gatherings where he is a huge hit and it’s been great to see him happy.
For me, about to turn 70, it is inspiring to read about and see that there is plenty of life still to be had.

comments.name: J Hughes
comments.body: I’m sure an elderly neighbor down the hall or on a park bench is just as funny and inspiring irl without being produced and marketed through social media. If we all get off our phone and interact with each other, content creators would be a thing of the past .

comments.name: HJS
comments.body: I'm old/elderly/senior. Keeping up with what I consider a generally vapid media afflicted generation isn't something I aspire to. When I was young, I had fabulous adventures in much more interesting times. Now, well, I keep on truckin'!

articles.title: Hating Matcha, Yet Loving Life, Made Him a TikTok Star at 89
articles.summary: Werner Kalecinski is a social media sensation among young Germans. How did he go from heartbroken widower to partying on a yacht?

comments.name: GG
comments.body: It really makes one feel for Prince William. No wonder he said 2024 was the worst of his life. Taking care of Princess Catherine and their three young children, trying to shield the kids from anxiety and scrutiny, all with the pressure of the throne hanging over his head? And that's without taking into account the international "Where's Kate" trolling and bullying campaign directed at him and the Princess of Wales. It's extraordinary that he came through to the other side.

comments.name: Innocent Bystander
comments.body: As to why Charles disclosed that he had cancer but not the specific kind of cancer: the British tabloids are cruelly invasive and their comments sections allow folks to go at it with every kind of speculation.  While the late Queen Elizabeth was respectfully off limits, following an older script going back centuries, every other member of the royal family surrounding her has been fair game at some point.  As the spares self-destructed (Margaret, Andrew and Harry), there was glee on Fleet Street and a rush to stoke the downfall.  Even Charles as the Prince of Wales was tabloid fodder.  He was torn apart during the Diana soap opera years, while she was sanctified.  The amount of information Charles has announced about his cancer allows his diagnosis to lend itself to his public service message about the disease, while he also preserves his dignity and the dignity of his office.  The same goes for the Princess of Wales, who gets magnifying glass goings over of her body every time she appears in public.  She is lovely and people do stare at her outward presence, and that's quite enough voyeurism.  No need for nosy parkers to speculate about a missing womb or breast or whatever while passing off their intrusiveness as concern for her well being.

comments.name: Not Your Average Joe
comments.body: Diagnosed with Bladder Cancer and having just completed the regimen of Keytruda and Padcev, I have not been silent and, when asked, admit to nausea, weight loss and more.  My prognosis is "Cured" with close monitoring going forward. I am grateful for my medical team that is saving my life and the Almighty.  Prayers for all who suffer.

comments.name: Fran
comments.body: Even royals are in the end only people.

comments.name: Marty Dogwood
comments.body: The big "C" is a life changer. Best to share. To borrow the famous line from Streisand, "People need People".

comments.name: John
comments.body: Cancer treatment can be really rough. Charles was trained early to "suck it up" and not complain about physical hardship. I don't think many American kids, then or now, would last more than a week at Gordonstoun, the boarding school he was sent off to at 13. He has faults, like any human, but there is much about him to admire and learn from.

comments.name: AB
comments.body: I have friends recently diagnosed with aggressive cancer.  They've decided to tell just a few people because they don't want to be defined by the diagnosis.  Besides, whose business is it but theirs.

comments.name: Jeffhnit
comments.body: It is always a personal decision on how much to share about a medical condition. Hat’s off to those who use their position or prominence to share their cancer story and encourage others to get checked to find cancer in early stages when many times treatments are more successful.

articles.title: Queen Camilla Says It Was ‘Difficult’ to Keep Charles’s Cancer a Secret
articles.summary: “I was just longing to let it out,” Camilla said in rare public comments about the king’s 2024 diagnosis, which was not immediately revealed. “But obviously I couldn’t.”

comments.name: Dude
comments.body: MRNA is another technology the US will fall behind on due to poor leadership, funding, and forethought.  The rest of the world is leaving us behind and Americans keep electing incompetence.

comments.name: Arthur
comments.body: I read in SeekingAlpha that Trump apparently made a bunch of money off Moderna. How come no one‘s talking about this?

comments.name: Cathy
comments.body: Googling the Moderna Melanoma trial results brings up startling few pieces about the actual trial results and primarily articles about the impact of the trial results on the stock price.  NYT, how about long pieces about the trial and its potential rather than the financial impact!?

comments.name: Chris
comments.body: Has Kennedy cited any evidence to justify his "hostility" to MRNA research? I imagine his opposition would disappear should he or a family member be diagnosed with an illness that MRNA could treat.

comments.name: poslug
comments.body:
RFK Jr canceled hundreds of millions of grants to develop mRNA cures. Cures less devastating than the current ones and some to shut down developing a disease. 

Do you think you or your family would not want such a benefit from out modern science based nation or do you want MAHA's untested supplements hawked online?

RFK Jr is your enemy and all those in his circle pushing untested supplements to line their pockets.

comments.name: Kate A.
comments.body:
There is a man on my myeloma listserv participating in this very clinical trial with the mRNA technology and after only three cycles, he is MRD negative. This is revolutionary technology and should be supported by our government wholeheartedly.
Thank god for innovative companies like Moderna and Merck!  Because Merck also makes KeyTruda, they stand to make a boatload of $$$ if this vaccine can be paired with their very lucrative Keytruda, an immunotherapy drug used in a dozen cancers and as they say in their TV ads, "a chance to live longer."
Kudos to them both and THANK YOU!!!

comments.name: CH
comments.body: Where is the outrage against these vaccines? Why aren't they demanding a clinical trial comparing the new medicines to Ivermectin? It's interesting that the conspiracy theory crowd is so opposed to treating infectious diseases, but ok with treating cancer.

comments.name: Bill White
comments.body:
Of course this is great news for cancer treatment, but the disturbing news is the Trump-Kennedy coterie canceling mRNA research and development of vaccines for contagious diseases. Recall how COVID came out of nowhere; we may be only 1 mutation away from a bird flu pandemic. Cancelling that research is beyond irresponsible.
This cancer vaccine shows the advantage of mRNA technology: just sub in a couple of nucleotides in the RNA molecule and you relatively quickly have a highly targeted vaccine. 
This is important for diseases such as flu, where the virus evolves rapidly and conventional vaccines are 6 months behind on that evolution.
As for COVID, I will continue to get the Moderna vaccine annually and also hope to get the new mRNA flu vaccine this season.

articles.title: How Moderna Nearly Tripled Its Stock Price in a Single Day
articles.summary: The company’s fortunes cratered as demand for Covid-19 vaccines plummeted. But it was busy working on something else.

comments.name: John
comments.body: Archaeology has long moved past Schliemann's artifact hunting. The most important people on the job are the surveyors--the ones recording the strata, the relationships between found objects and their matrices, and "meaningless" gaps in the record.

comments.name: Bruce Williams
comments.body: Whatever happens, it has to be remembered that neither Lord Elgin nor Schliemann nor anybody else could have moved anything in the Ottoman Empire without the knowledge and consent, one way or another, of the Porte.  It's also true that the Ottoman authorities were eager to placate the West because they had just been defeated by Russia and were under even greater pressure thereafter.  Finally, it's also true that the Archaeological Museum in Istanbul has a major collection of objects taken from Lebanon, most notably, the Alexander Sarcophagus, a transcendent masterpiece.  It won't be resolved by us or in these pages.

comments.name: Brad
comments.body: It belongs to Turkey because that is where Troy was located.  No other destination is possible.

comments.name: Horace
comments.body: Not every object has to remain in the geographical place where it was found. And many mistakes have been made in "returning" objects. For example sending Tibetan objects to China, when China is erasing Tibetan culture. When a country has many examples of certain types of artifacts I see no reason why a relatively small sample of such objects can't be kept in museums around the world, where everyone can appreciate them.  Determining the rightful owners of ancient artifacts is not always so simple as locating the geographical source, as when the current inhabitants may be descended from the enemies of the original artisans. It happens often.

comments.name: Luigi Grassi
comments.body: The most famous case for restitution is, of course, that of the so- called Elgin Marbles, the sculptures from the Parthenon, which England and Greece have been haggling over for years.

comments.name: Gandalf the Blue
comments.body:
I'm on the side of returning the artifacts to the site from which they were looted.  Yes, looted. 

European "adventurers" traveled all over the world taking stuff that didn't belong to them. What gave them the right to take it, sell or donate it, and whoever has it now, keep it?

I want to see all the pieces of the Parthenon brought back to Athens and put on display in the wonderful museum near the Acropolis. Why should the Brits have it? (And a lot of other stuff of antiquity they looted and are now on display at the  British Museum.) 

Tourism is big business, and if we ever get past the present chaos and turmoil and onto a sound path of shared prosperity for the world around, not just western powers or China, tourism will become even bigger. People will want to see everything to do with Troy at the site.

Just ask yourself this: What would Indiana Jones do?

It's difficult to drive any highway in the US without seeing multiple billboards with photos of lawyers, each promising big "wins" for anyone in an auto accident. These attempts to inflate the insurance payout via litigation drive up the cost of insurance for everyone.  Even if these attorneys are unsuccessful, the cost of defending against the fraudulent claims is borne by the insurance company and passed along in the form of increased premiums.  

It's a variation on the tort bar's "Sue and Settle" game that threatens companies with questionable class actions by making it cheaper to settle than litigate.

I played with the Doctor software at MIT back around 1967 or '68.  First impression was that it was fantastic, and might even pass Turing's test.  

But then I decided to see what it was actually doing, so I typed in the same statement a bunch of times.  It cycled through a set of responses and then cycled through them again.  Aha--fails Turing's test.

But unless you were trying to get your arms around what was going on, it could seem eerily realistic.  Kinda like the current batch of AIs.  Today's are vastly more realistic and generate lines of thought that I didn't.  Doctor didn't really do that.

Want to find out whether you're interacting with a computer or a human?  Ask it.  They usually tell the truth.
